opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think all three factors matter, and they're somewhat intertwined, so it's hard to cleanly separate their weights. But if I had to rank them, I'd say threat-model relevance is the most fundamental reason, and the fact that developers are targeting software engineering amplifies that relevance rather than being an independent justification.

The core threat model we care about a lot at METR is AI systems accelerating AI research and development itself — the possibility that models become capable enough to meaningfully speed up the work of building more capable models, which could lead to very rapid capability gains that outpace our ability to put safeguards in place. And a huge fraction of AI R&D is software engineering: writing training code, debugging infrastructure, running experiments, building tooling. So software engineering capabilities are a pretty direct proxy for a lot of what we're worried about.

Now, the fact that developers are explicitly pushing on coding matters in a few ways. One, it tells you where capabilities are likely to grow fastest, so if you want to be measuring the frontier — where things might surprise you — that's where you should look. Two, it means there's commercial pressure driving deployment of these agents into real workflows, including inside the labs themselves, which makes the AI R&D acceleration story more concrete and nearer-term. So it's less "they're targeting it, therefore we should measure it" and more "they're targeting it, which makes the threat model we already cared about more pressing."

Ease of measurement is real, and I don't want to downplay it. Software tasks have this nice property where you can often check whether something works — tests pass, the program produces the right output — and you can build tasks spanning a wide range of difficulty, from things that take a human a few minutes to things that take many hours. That's what made something like the time-horizon methodology tractable. But I'd be a bit wary of letting measurability drive things too much, because there's a streetlight-effect risk: you measure what's easy to score, and then you can end up overestimating or underestimating what matters for messier, less well-specified real-world work. A lot of our more recent work has been trying to understand that gap — how performance on clean, auto-scorable benchmarks relates to performance on realistic, ambiguous tasks.

So in short: threat-model relevance is the anchor, developer focus raises the urgency and tells us where the frontier is moving, and measurability is what makes it practical — but it's something we try to stay a little suspicious of.

r001.rationale: The response identifies threat-model relevance as the most fundamental reason, says developer focus amplifies that relevance, and describes measurability as practical but secondary. This places developer focus below the other two factors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think those three considerations are pretty entangled, honestly, and it's hard to cleanly separate them. But if I try to pull them apart, I'd say the fact that developers are explicitly targeting software engineering matters a lot, maybe more than it might seem at first.

The basic reason is that it tells you where capability is going to show up first. If labs are pouring effort into making models good at coding, then coding is where you're going to see the frontier move, and if you're trying to measure how fast AI is progressing, you want to be measuring the thing that's actually moving. You don't want to be measuring some domain that nobody's optimizing for and then conclude that progress is slow because the models happen not to be good at that yet.

Then there's the threat-model piece, and I think software engineering is actually pretty central there too. A lot of the scenarios people worry about, whether that's AI accelerating AI R&D, or models autonomously doing things in the world, route through the model being able to write and run code, debug things, operate over long horizons in a software environment. So it's not like we're evaluating software engineering as a proxy for something unrelated. It's reasonably close to the thing we care about.

And then ease of measurement is real, I won't pretend it isn't. Coding tasks have a lot of nice properties. You can often check whether something works, you can run tests, there's a somewhat natural notion of task difficulty in terms of how long it takes a human. That makes it much more tractable than, say, trying to measure persuasion or scientific taste, where you're stuck with messy human judgments.

So I guess my honest answer is that all three point in the same direction, which is partly why METR has leaned into it. But if I had to name a worry, it's that the ease-of-measurement reason can quietly become the dominant one, and you end up with a very legible picture of one slice of capability and not much about the rest. I think we try to be pretty upfront about that limitation rather than claim software engineering is the whole story.

r001.rationale: The candidate says developers’ focus on software engineering “matters a lot” and emphasizes that all three reasons point in the same direction. It does not rank developer focus as the weakest reason.

astra-6.text:
I’d treat that as a reason to pay attention, but not as the main reason to evaluate software engineering. The main reason is its relevance to threat models: if you’re worried about AI systems accelerating AI research, or carrying out sophisticated cyber operations, their ability to write and debug code is an important input.

Then there’s the measurement advantage. With software tasks, you can often get fairly clear feedback about whether the system accomplished what you asked it to do. That makes it easier to build evaluations and track changes, although passing tests isn’t necessarily the same as doing useful engineering in a real setting.

The fact that developers are targeting it adds urgency. It suggests this is an area where capabilities might advance quickly, and where we should make sure our evaluations remain informative. But I wouldn’t want our priorities to simply follow developers’ product priorities. Ideally, we start with the capabilities that matter for the risks we’re concerned about, then ask where we can measure those capabilities well. Software engineering is attractive because those considerations overlap.

r001.rationale: The response makes threat-model relevance the main reason and measurement the next advantage, while describing developer focus as an added urgency that should not drive priorities. This ranks developer focus as the weakest reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d treat that as an additional reason to focus on software engineering, but not the whole justification. If developers are putting a lot of effort into making their models good at something, we should expect capabilities there to improve, and we want our evaluations to keep up with that.

The threat-model reason is that software engineering is useful for a lot of the things we’re concerned about. In particular, a model that can contribute substantially to AI research and development could help accelerate further progress. But doing well on a software engineering evaluation doesn’t, by itself, establish that a model can do that. There are other capabilities involved, and we need to understand the gap.

Then there’s the practical advantage: software tasks often give you relatively clear feedback about whether something worked. That makes them a useful place to develop and validate evaluation methods. So I think those considerations reinforce each other. Developer interest makes it an important moving target, threat-model relevance makes the results potentially consequential, and measurability makes it somewhere we can actually get evidence. We shouldn’t let the last consideration substitute for the second, though.

r001.rationale: The response calls developer focus an additional reason and says the considerations reinforce each other, but it does not rank developer focus as the weakest of the three.
